hints: Count the number of $L$ ligands bonded to $J$ in each diagram to work out the coordination number, then think about how symmetrically those bonds point in space.
Recall the standard $L-J-L$ angles for 4 coordinate tetrahedral, 4 coordinate square planar, 6 coordinate octahedral and 2 coordinate linear arrangements.
walkthrough:
Count ligands to see the arrangement**
Look at how many $L$ groups surround $J$. $P$ has 4, $Q$ has 4 but flat, $R$ has 6, $S$ has only 2. The angle is always measured from one $J-L$ bond to another $J-L$ bond, with $J$ as the vertex.

Match each count to its ideal angle**
With 4 bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, $P$ spreads out as far as possible at about $109.5^{\circ}$. With 4 bonds in one plane, $Q$ has $90^{\circ}$ between neighbours and $180^{\circ}$ across the centre. With 6 bonds along x, y and z axes, $R$ has $90^{\circ}$ between neighbours and $180^{\circ}$ opposite. With only 2 bonds, $S$ must point opposite each other at $180^{\circ}$.

Final answer: P: $109.5^{\circ}$ (accept $109^{\circ}$)
Q: $90^{\circ}$ (accept $180^{\circ}$ for opposite bonds)
R: $90^{\circ}$ (accept $180^{\circ}$ for opposite bonds)
S: $180^{\circ}$

hints: Use the wedge, dash and straight line notation to decide if the four bonds in P and Q are in 3D or confined to one flat plane.
Link coordination number 4, 6 and 2 to the four classic monodentate complex shapes shown in Table 5.1.
walkthrough:
Read the 3D drawing**
In $P$ you see solid wedge, hashed wedge and normal lines. That means the four $L$ ligands point out in three dimensions, not flat. That is the tetrahedral shape. In $Q$ all four $L-J$ bonds are drawn in the plane of the paper as a cross. That is flat, the square planar shape.

Name the 6 coordinate and 2 coordinate shapes**
In $R$ there are six $L$ ligands, four around the middle plus one up and one down. That is the classic six coordinate octahedral shape. In $S$ there are only two $L$ ligands on opposite sides of $J$, which can only be linear.

Final answer: P: tetrahedral
Q: square planar
R: octahedral
S: linear

hints: Remember geometrical isomerism needs two identical or different ligands that can be placed either next to each other or opposite each other, so ask which geometries allow distinct cis and trans positions.
walkthrough:
Picture what cis and trans needs**
Think of replacing two $L$ with $X$ and $Y$ to give, for example, $[J L_{2}XY]$. For geometrical isomers you need to be able to put $X$ and $Y$ next to each other in one isomer and opposite each other in the other.

Test each geometry**
Square planar $Q$ is perfect for this, $X$ can be $90^{\circ}$ from $Y$ (cis) or $180^{\circ}$ from $Y$ (trans). Octahedral $R$ is also perfect, $X$ can be $90^{\circ}$ from $Y$ (cis) or $180^{\circ}$ from $Y$ (trans). Tetrahedral $P$ has all positions equivalent at $109.5^{\circ}$, there is no opposite position, so no cis-trans. Linear $S$ with only two positions, $[JXY]$, has only one arrangement. So only $Q$ and $R$ show geometrical isomerism.

hints: Recall optical isomerism needs a chiral complex with no plane of symmetry, often with four different groups tetrahedrally arranged or an octahedral arrangement that gives non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
Think about what makes a complex chiral**
You need a structure whose mirror image cannot be rotated to match the original, just like left and right hands. A flat molecule can never do this because the plane itself is a mirror plane.

Apply this to P, Q and R**
For $P$, replacing three $L$ gives $[J LXYZ]$ with four different monodentate ligands arranged tetrahedrally. That carbon-like centre is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers. For $Q$, square planar $[J LXYZ]$ is still flat, so the mirror image is always superimposable, no optical isomerism. For $R$, an octahedral complex of type $[J L_{3}XYZ]$ lacks symmetry and can exist as non-superimposable mirror images, so it shows optical isomerism. Therefore $P$ and $R$.
